segments.t: DE
Release notesKTPH000
What changed in the current release. The version this guide was built for is shown in the footer.
TerminalKTPH000

KTPH010Session isolation, sandboxed local shells and incognito sessionsKTPH011 — a connection, a folder of the Connection Manager or KTPH012Settings → Security → Session isolationKTPH013 can now choose how far a terminal session is kept apart from korTTY and the other tabs: KTPH014NoneKTPH015, KTPH016Own processKTPH017 or KTPH018Own process + sandboxKTPH019. In the sandbox (KTPH000 on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux, checked by a self-test before it counts) a local shell or the native KTPH001 cannot read korTTY's configuration folder, your SSH and GnuPG keys or the keychains and writes only to its working folder and temporary files; An isolated SSH session runs in a KTPH020session workerKTPH021, a process of its own that holds the server connection while your private key stays in korTTY, which signs for it; SFTP, file drops, the AI agent and KTPH002/KTPH003/KTPH004 tunnels work as before, and KTPH022Tools → Session Processes...KTPH023 lists the workers with their memory and CPU and can end one. The built-in Mosh client runs isolated in a session worker as well, its sandbox limited to the UDP port of the session. On Linux a sandboxed worker has no network of its own: korTTY connects it only to the server and jump server of its connection. The tab shows a shield: an outline for an own process, filled for a sandbox, with an exclamation mark when a sandbox was asked for but is not active. A KTPH024strict terminal modeKTPH025, automatic in a sandbox, drops clipboard access, non-web links, spoofing titles and device control strings a hostile server could send. An KTPH026incognito sessionKTPH027 — per connection or with KTPH028File → New Incognito Session…KTPH029, with or without isolation — writes no log, journal or recording, leaves no Recently Closed entry and is not restored after a restart; its tab shows a spy. An administrator can demand a minimum with KTPH005 and forbid incognito sessions with KTPH006. A script can open a saved connection with KTPH007, with KTPH008 and KTPH009 if it likes, never below the organization's minimum. See KTPH030Session isolationKTPH031.

KTPH007Coding agentsKTPH008 — korTTY recognises Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI in local shell tabs and classifies each pane as working, blocked on a question, done or idle, and now shows it everywhere: a glyph in the tab title, chips, accent bars, rollups and pane rows in the dashboard (which expands to a waiting agent and offers Send Enter / Esc / Interrupt in the context menu), a dockable KTPH009Coding AgentsKTPH010 panel (KTPH011View → Coding AgentsKTPH012, KTPH013KTPH001KTPH014+KTPH015KTPH002KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH003KTPH018) listing every agent of every window with one-click answers (y, n, Enter, Esc, ↑, ↓, Ctrl+C), Explain, Rename and a prompt box, a status-bar strip, KTPH019KTPH004KTPH020+KTPH021KTPH005KTPH022+KTPH023KTPH006KTPH024 to jump to the next waiting agent, a badge with the number of waiting agents on the app icon (Dock, Windows taskbar, KDE/Ubuntu launcher; window title elsewhere) and a desktop notification when an agent needs a decision or finishes while you are not looking at its pane. Detection reads the terminal screen locally and can be switched off in KTPH025Settings → Terminal → Coding agentsKTPH026, where the badge and the notifications have their own toggles; the rules are JSON files you can override under KTPH000. See KTPH027Coding agentsKTPH028.

KTPH004Control API and KTPH000KTPH005 — korTTY can now open a local socket so a script or a coding agent on the same computer can list your windows, read any pane, type into it, wait for output, split a local shell, and drive a detected coding agent. It is KTPH006off by defaultKTPH007 and is switched on under KTPH008Settings → Terminal → Control APIKTPH009, where a status line reports what the listener is actually doing. Nothing is reachable over the network and no other user of the computer can connect: the endpoint lives in an owner-only KTPH001 directory and needs a token that is regenerated on every start. Every action is logged with byte counts only, never terminal text, and the first time a program types into a pane you get one desktop notification, so a takeover is never silent. An administrator can deny the feature outright with the KTPH002 policy key. The KTPH003 client ships beside the application in every native package and handles discovery, authentication and exit codes for you. See KTPH010Control APIKTPH011 and KTPH012Control CLIKTPH013.

KTPH002korTTY as an MCP server for AI assistantsKTPH003 — KTPH000 lets an AI assistant that speaks the Model Context Protocol list your tabs, panes and coding agents, read a pane and wait for output in it. It runs as a child process of the assistant over stdio, opens no network port and reaches korTTY through the local Control API. It is KTPH004read-only and off by defaultKTPH005: switch it on with KTPH006MCP serverKTPH007 under KTPH008Settings → Terminal → Control APIKTPH009, below the Control API checkbox. Everything an assistant reads has known secrets masked and is capped at 2,000 lines and 64,000 characters. A second switch, KTPH010Allow write toolsKTPH011, also offers tools that type text, run a command or press keys in a pane, and korTTY asks you before every one of those writes; you can allow plain text for one pane for the rest of the session, but running a line always asks. Panes with a slow paste, a full-screen program, a nested login, broadcast or multi-exec, or a coding agent are refused. An administrator can deny the whole feature with the KTPH001 policy key, and anonymous usage statistics, if you allowed them, report which tools are used and how the calls ended, never what they read or typed. See KTPH012Serving MCP clientsKTPH013 and KTPH014MCP clientsKTPH015.

KTPH006Prompts and Control API pastes can no longer end their bracketed paste earlyKTPH007 — a bracketed-paste end marker (KTPH000, or its 8-bit form in a single-byte encoding) inside the text of a coding-agent prompt or a bracketed KTPH001 closed the paste korTTY had wrapped around it, so every following line reached the program as typed input and was submitted on its own. korTTY now removes the start and end markers from every prompt and from the text of a bracketed KTPH002, including markers that only form once an inner one is removed and, in a Windows-1252 pane, the KTPH003 that this encoding sends as the 8-bit introducer; an unbracketed KTPH004 or KTPH005 still keeps them. See KTPH008Typing into a paneKTPH009.

KTPH002Terminal pastes can no longer end their bracketed paste earlyKTPH003 — korTTY passed pasted text to the terminal unchanged, so a bracketed-paste end marker (KTPH000) inside it closed the paste the terminal wrapped around it, and every following line reached the shell as typed input and ran on its own. Every terminal paste (the paste shortcut, KTPH004Edit → PasteKTPH005, KTPH006PasteKTPH007 in the right-click menu and a middle-click) now goes through korTTY, which removes the start and end markers from the text, including their 8-bit form in a single-byte character encoding, before it wraps the paste itself. A pane also no longer keeps bracketed paste switched on after a reconnect or a terminal reset (KTPH001), which wrapped pastes in markers that the next program might not understand. See KTPH008Pasting textKTPH009.

KTPH001Paste protectionKTPH002 — a terminal paste that could run commands or hide something now asks first. A paste with line breaks asks unless the program in the pane uses bracketed paste, a paste with control characters (such as Escape or Ctrl+C) or invisible direction-changing characters asks even then, and a paste larger than 5 KiB always asks. The dialog shows the pane, the number of lines, the size, the reasons and a preview in which hidden characters are visible; KTPH003CancelKTPH004 is the default button, so pressing KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006 by habit never pastes. Choose when it asks under KTPH007Settings → Terminal → Paste protectionKTPH008: KTPH009AlwaysKTPH010 asks for every paste with a line break, KTPH011OffKTPH012 only keeps the size check, and a size of 0 turns that off. See KTPH013Paste protectionKTPH014.

KTPH001Paste line by line into slow devicesKTPH002 — switches, routers and console servers behind SSH can lose input that arrives too fast, so a pasted configuration arrived with characters or lines missing. KTPH003Settings → Terminal → Paste protection → Pause after each pasted lineKTPH004 (0 to 1,000 ms, off by default) now sends a paste with several lines one line at a time with that pause. The pane shows how far the paste is, takes no keys meanwhile so nothing you type lands between two lines, and KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006 stops the rest; broadcast mode leaves the pane out until it is done. See KTPH007Pasting into slow devicesKTPH008.

KTPH000Drop text onto a terminalKTPH001 — text dragged from a browser, an editor or another korTTY window and dropped onto a terminal was ignored; only files were taken, to be copied to the server. Dropped text is now pasted into the pane under the pointer, which becomes the focused pane, through paste protection like any other paste, and it is always copied, so the application you drag from keeps it. The setting is now called KTPH002Settings → Terminal → Allow drag and drop into the terminalKTPH003 and covers files and text; with the enterprise policy's internal clipboard mode, text from other applications is refused. See KTPH004Dropping textKTPH005.

KTPH003Files dropped onto a terminal land where you dropped them, and only thereKTPH004 — a file drop always went to the pane you had last clicked, even when you dropped it onto another pane of a split tab; it now goes to the pane under the pointer, which becomes the focused pane. After KTPH000, KTPH001 or a nested KTPH002 the files were still uploaded with the tab's own login into the directory the inner shell reported, which may belong to another user or host; korTTY now refuses such a drop with a message, and KTPH005Copy as file(s) to terminal directoryKTPH006 and KTPH007Copy folder to terminal directoryKTPH008 in the Snippet Manager do the same. A dropped folder containing a link to one of its parent folders no longer makes the copy run until it fails: links to folders are skipped and counted in the progress window, while links to files are still copied with their content. Each drop also kept one SFTP channel of the terminal's SSH session open until the tab closed, so after many drops the server could refuse new channels; the channel is now closed when the copy ends, and a drop onto a session that has just closed says so instead of failing with an internal error. See KTPH009Dropping textKTPH010.

KTPH003A shell on another host is recognised from its directory reportsKTPH004 — shells that report their directory with OSC 7 also name their host. korTTY now remembers the host of the first report of your own session and, when a later report names another host, no longer moves the tracked terminal directory there and treats the pane as running elsewhere: file drops and snippet copies are refused as after KTPH000 or a nested KTPH001, until the original host reports again or the tab reconnects. The full name of the host, KTPH002 and reports without a host count as the same host. See KTPH005Dropping textKTPH006.

KTPH000Busy sessions on slow links are no longer cut off as lostKTPH001 — korTTY declared an SSH connection lost when two liveness probes in a row went unanswered, even when the server was still sending data and the reply was only queued behind it, for example a large output or a file transfer over a slow link. An unanswered probe now only counts while nothing arrives from the server at all, so such a session stays open, and a dead network is still noticed within about ten seconds. See KTPH002Connection loss and automatic reconnectKTPH003.

KTPH000Command timestamps stay on their command linesKTPH001 — once the scrollback had reached its limit, the marks in the command timestamp sidebar drifted one row further from their command with every new line of output, and a new prompt on the bottom row got no mark of its own. Marks now move with their lines, disappear when their line leaves the scrollback, and are removed by KTPH002Clear BufferKTPH003. The dates in the sidebar and its hover popup follow the UI language instead of a fixed German order, and KTPH004DuplicateKTPH005 and KTPH006No GroupKTPH007 in the tab context menu are translated instead of always German. See KTPH008Terminal settingsKTPH009.

KTPH000Anonymous usage statistics now cover coding agents and the Control APIKTPH001 — if you allowed anonymous statistics, korTTY also reports which agent kinds are detected, how often agent notifications fire, which Control API methods are used and whether the coding-agent and Control API settings are on. Only kinds, states, method names and counts are sent — never terminal text, prompts or pane names. See KTPH002Anonymous dataKTPH003.

KTPH000Anonymous usage statistics now cover the command palette, multi-exec and session restoreKTPH001 — if you allowed anonymous statistics, korTTY also reports which kind of command palette row you run, when you turn multi-exec on or off and how far it reaches, when the previous session is restored and how, and whether you changed the quick-select letters or patterns, the tab-title and tab-order switches or any shortcut. Only kinds, flags and rounded counts are sent — never search text, names, hosts, patterns or what you type. See KTPH002Anonymous dataKTPH003.

KTPH002Cmd/Ctrl+W and the Dashboard's Close ask before closing a busy terminalKTPH003 — the tab's close button asks before it closes a tab with split panes or a command that is still running, but KTPH004Close TabKTPH005 (KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 on macOS, KTPH010File → Close TabKTPH011) and KTPH012CloseKTPH013 in the Dashboard closed such a tab straight away and ended the running command. All three now ask the same question; an idle terminal at its prompt still closes immediately, and a connection set to KTPH014Close tab without confirmationKTPH015 never asks. A terminal closed with KTPH016Close TabKTPH017, the Dashboard's KTPH018CloseKTPH019 or KTPH020Close All TabsKTPH021 is now also released like one closed with its close button, instead of staying in memory with its status-bar timer still running. See KTPH022Working with tabsKTPH023.

KTPH004Tabs that close on their own are fully releasedKTPH005 — when a split pane was left as the last pane and its shell exited, or KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 closed a local cmd or PowerShell tab, the tab closed without the cleanup its close button runs: korTTY still counted that pane as connected, so with KTPH010Configuration KTPH016 Prevent System SleepKTPH011 checked the computer was kept awake, and a shell closed with KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 kept running in the background. Such tabs now close exactly like a tab closed with its close button.

KTPH022Navigation keys reach programs the way they expect themKTPH023 — korTTY used to send the arrow keys, Tab, Home/End, Page Up/Down, Insert/Delete and the F-keys as fixed sequences without their modifiers, so KTPH024KTPH002KTPH025+KTPH026KTPH003KTPH027 and KTPH028KTPH004KTPH029+KTPH030KTPH005KTPH031 arrived as plain Left and Tab and KTPH032KTPH006KTPH033+KTPH034KTPH007KTPH035 as F1. They are now encoded the xterm way and follow the program's cursor-key mode, so word movement (KTPH036KTPH008KTPH037+KTPH038KTPH009KTPH039 / KTPH040KTPH010KTPH041+KTPH042KTPH011KTPH043, KTPH044KTPH012KTPH045+KTPH046KTPH013KTPH047 / KTPH048KTPH014KTPH049+KTPH050KTPH015KTPH051 on macOS) and back-tab work in the shell, KTPH000 and KTPH001. KTPH052KTPH016KTPH053+KTPH054KTPH017KTPH055 / KTPH056KTPH018KTPH057+KTPH058KTPH019KTPH059 now scroll korTTY's scrollback, KTPH060KTPH020KTPH061+KTPH062KTPH021KTPH063 switches tabs while the terminal has the focus, editing the find bar's search text no longer types into the shell, and broadcast mode mirrors these keys to every pane, encoded for each. See KTPH064Keyboard shortcutsKTPH065.

KTPH000Broadcast mode no longer freezes the window when one server stallsKTPH001 — the keys mirrored into the other panes were sent on the thread that draws the window, so a pane whose SSH connection had stopped responding froze korTTY on every keystroke. They are now sent in the background, still in the order you typed them for each pane, so only the stalled pane waits while the window and the other panes keep reacting. See KTPH002Broadcast modeKTPH003.

KTPH003Broadcast mode keeps AI agents and passwords where they belongKTPH004 — the keys typed in broadcast mode reached every pane of the tab, so KTPH000 and KTPH005KTPH001KTPH006 started an AI agent run in each pane, a mirrored KTPH007KTPH002KTPH008 could approve what a coding agent waiting for a decision asked in another pane, and a sudo password typed in one pane ran as a command in the panes at an ordinary prompt, where it stayed in their shell history and session journal. Now the agent shortcut starts a run only in the pane you type in, panes where an AI agent runs or a coding agent waits for your decision get no mirrored keys (the KTPH009ExtrasKTPH010 submenu of a pane's right-click menu says how many are left out), and while you type at a password prompt your keys go only to the panes at a password prompt too. See KTPH011Broadcast modeKTPH012.

KTPH010Copying and pasting in broadcast mode no longer reaches the other panesKTPH011 — on Windows and Linux, KTPH012KTPH000KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH001KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH002KTPH017 and KTPH018KTPH003KTPH019+KTPH020KTPH004KTPH021+KTPH022KTPH005KTPH023 still produce the control character of KTPH024KTPH006KTPH025+KTPH026KTPH007KTPH027 or KTPH028KTPH008KTPH029+KTPH030KTPH009KTPH031, and broadcast mode sent it to the other panes of the tab: copying a selection interrupted the program running in each of them, and pasting made their shells insert the next key literally. A key now goes to the other panes only when the pane you type in sends it to its own program as well, which also keeps the keys of menu commands out of them. See KTPH032Broadcast modeKTPH033.

KTPH009Ctrl+L and Ctrl+F reach the shell on Windows and LinuxKTPH010 — the terminal's own Clear Buffer and Find took these keys, so KTPH011KTPH001KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014 wiped the scrollback instead of redrawing the screen in bash, psql or a REPL, and KTPH015KTPH003KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH004KTPH018 never moved the cursor forward or paged forward in KTPH000. Both keys now go to the shell; Clear Buffer and Find stay in the terminal's right-click menu and Find in KTPH019Edit → Find…KTPH020, while KTPH021KTPH005KTPH022+KTPH023KTPH006KTPH024 and KTPH025KTPH007KTPH026+KTPH027KTPH008KTPH028 on macOS are unchanged. On Linux a selection copied automatically also becomes the X11 primary selection, so a middle-click pastes it in other applications. See KTPH029Keyboard shortcutsKTPH030.

KTPH000Bold text in bright colorsKTPH001 — KTPH002Settings → Terminal → Bold textKTPH003 now chooses how text that a program prints in bold is drawn: in a bold font (the default, as before), in the bright variant of its color the way xterm does, or both. Bright colors come from your palette on the Colors tab and apply to every open terminal and to terminal recordings as soon as you save. It replaces the KTPH004Bold as bright colorKTPH005 switch, which only ever affected recordings; with the terminal engine SithTermFX 1.2.4. See KTPH006TerminalKTPH007.

KTPH000The terminal find bar speaks your languageKTPH001 — the find bar of a terminal pane (KTPH002Edit → Find...KTPH003) showed its texts in English whatever language korTTY used. Its search field, the KTPH004Ignore caseKTPH005 switch, the match count such as KTPH0063 of 12KTPH007, KTPH008No matchesKTPH009 and the tooltips of the next and previous buttons now follow the language set in korTTY, with the terminal engine SithTermFX 1.2.4. See KTPH010TerminalKTPH011.

KTPH000The ANSI colors and the selection color on the Colors tab now take effectKTPH001 — the 16 color pickers in KTPH002Settings → ColorsKTPH003 were never saved, and the terminal ignored the KTPH004SelectionKTPH005 color too. Both now apply to every open terminal as soon as you save, and terminal recordings use the same colors as the screen. Settings you never changed keep the built-in palette and inverse-video selection, so nothing looks different until you customize a color. See KTPH006ColorsKTPH007.

KTPH000Menu commands follow the pane you type inKTPH001 — in a split tab, KTPH002Edit → CopyKTPH003, KTPH004Edit → PasteKTPH005, KTPH006Edit → Find...KTPH007, the AI actions and a recording of the active split used the pane you had last clicked. When the keyboard focus reached another pane some other way, for example with a middle-click, or stayed in the original pane after a split that showed a connection dialog, they acted on a different pane than the one receiving your typing, and closing one pane moved them to the first pane even when you were typing in another. They now use the pane that has the keyboard focus. See KTPH008Split operationsKTPH009.

KTPH000No pane close button on a tab with a single terminalKTPH001 — the × in a pane's top-right corner, meant for closing one pane of a split tab, also showed when the tab had only one pane, and clicking it there ended that terminal's session at once, without the question the tab's own close button asks before it closes a busy terminal. The × now shows only while the tab has more than one pane. See KTPH002Split operationsKTPH003.

KTPH000Same-server splits open on the pane's own serverKTPH001 — KTPH002Split Right (same server)KTPH003 and KTPH004Split Down (same server)KTPH005 always opened a session to the tab's server, so splitting a pane you had opened with KTPH006Split Right (new connection)KTPH007 or KTPH008Split Down (new connection)KTPH009 to another server put the new pane on the wrong host. They now open on the server of the pane you split, with the sign-in that pane used, and so do the panes split from it; the server access policy is checked for that server. See KTPH010Split operationsKTPH011.

KTPH004Move between split panes from the keyboard, and see which one has the focusKTPH005 — nothing showed which pane of a split tab the keyboard was in, and reaching another pane needed the mouse. A blue ring now marks the focused pane while the tab has two or more panes, and a dimmer ring stays on the pane the menu commands act on while you work in another window or panel; it never changes the size of the terminal. KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 (macOS) or KTPH010KTPH002KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH003KTPH013 (Windows, Linux) with an arrow key moves the focus to the pane on that side, and the new KTPH014View → PanesKTPH015 menu has the same commands, KTPH016Next PaneKTPH017, KTPH018Previous PaneKTPH019 and the tab's broadcast mode. With a single pane the keys still reach the program in the terminal. Screen readers name each pane KTPH020Pane 2 of 3KTPH021. See KTPH022Split operationsKTPH023.

KTPH011Split and close panes from the keyboard and the menu barKTPH012 — a pane could only be split or closed with the mouse, from its right-click menu or its ×. KTPH013KTPH000KTPH014+KTPH015KTPH001KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH002KTPH018 (macOS) or KTPH019KTPH003KTPH020+KTPH021KTPH004KTPH022+KTPH023KTPH005KTPH024 (Windows, Linux) now splits the pane the keyboard is in, on that pane's own server like KTPH025Split Right (same server)KTPH026: the new pane goes to the right of a wide pane and below a tall one, so repeated splits keep the panes roughly square, and the keyboard moves into it. KTPH027View → PanesKTPH028 has KTPH029Split PaneKTPH030, KTPH031Split RightKTPH032, KTPH033Split DownKTPH034 and KTPH035Close PaneKTPH036, which closes the pane the keyboard is in and is disabled in a tab's last pane. On Windows and Linux KTPH037KTPH006KTPH038+KTPH039KTPH007KTPH040+KTPH041KTPH008KTPH042 no longer reaches the shell; KTPH043KTPH009KTPH044+KTPH045KTPH010KTPH046 still does. See KTPH047Split operationsKTPH048.

KTPH007Zoom a split paneKTPH008 — KTPH009KTPH000KTPH010+KTPH011KTPH001KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014 (macOS) or KTPH015KTPH003KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH004KTPH018+KTPH019KTPH005KTPH020 (Windows, Linux), or KTPH021View → Panes → Zoom PaneKTPH022, lets the pane the keyboard is in fill the whole tab, and pressing it again shows all panes with every divider where it was. A badge on the zoomed pane says how many panes are hidden; they keep running at their size, so their programs see no resize. In broadcast mode the badge also says how many hidden panes still receive what you type, and turns amber. Splitting, closing or moving a pane and moving the focus to another pane show all panes again. With a single pane the key still reaches the program as KTPH023KTPH006KTPH024. See KTPH025Split operationsKTPH026.

KTPH000Multi-exec: type into chosen panes of several tabs and windows at onceKTPH001 — broadcast mode only reached the panes of one tab. Now you choose panes in any tab of any window, with KTPH002Extras → Multi-exec: Include This PaneKTPH003 in a pane's right-click menu, the tab's right-click menu, KTPH004View → Multi-execKTPH005 or a Dashboard row, and what you type in one of them goes to all the others, each key encoded for the program in each pane. Paste, snippets and input-method text stay in their pane, and the safety rules of broadcast mode apply: panes where an AI agent runs or a coding agent waits for your decision get nothing, an agent run starts only where you type, and a password typed at a prompt goes only to panes at a password prompt. There is no confirmation, but the chosen panes show an amber outline and a KTPH006Multi-execKTPH007 badge, their tabs and Dashboard rows an amber icon, and every window's status bar a chip with the number of panes, tabs and windows and a KTPH008StopKTPH009 link. In broadcast mode the panes and the tab now show the same markers. See KTPH010Multi-execKTPH011.

KTPH006Window shortcuts leave no character behind in the terminalKTPH007 — on Windows and Linux a key combination can still produce a typed character after korTTY has acted on it. For KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013 (Show / Hide Menu Bar) and KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019 (Terminal-only Fullscreen) korTTY now discards that character, as it already did for the zoom keys, so it can neither reach the shell nor be mirrored to the other panes in broadcast mode. See KTPH020Keyboard shortcutsKTPH021.

KTPH009Keyword highlighting in terminal outputKTPH010 — korTTY can now color errors and warnings, IP and MAC addresses, and the interface names and link states of switches and routers as output arrives, with three built-in rule sets (KTPH011Errors and warningsKTPH012, KTPH013Network addressesKTPH014, KTPH015Network devicesKTPH016). It is off until you switch it on: KTPH017KTPH003KTPH018+KTPH019KTPH004KTPH020+KTPH021KTPH005KTPH022 (KTPH023KTPH006KTPH024+KTPH025KTPH007KTPH026+KTPH027KTPH008KTPH028 on macOS) toggles it for the focused pane, and KTPH029View → HighlightingKTPH030 or KTPH031HighlightingKTPH032 in the terminal context menu picks the set. The choice applies to that pane for the running session; a new split inherits it. Highlighting only changes how text looks — copying, logs and the AI features see the original output — it skips full-screen programs such as KTPH000 and KTPH001, runs on a background thread so a fast KTPH002 keeps its speed, and gives each rule a time limit so a slow pattern cannot stall the terminal. See KTPH033Keyword highlightingKTPH034.

KTPH003A default highlighting rule set for every terminalKTPH004 — KTPH005Settings → Terminal → Keyword highlightingKTPH006 can now pick a rule set that every pane shows without a choice of its own, so highlighting is on in every new and open terminal without pressing the shortcut in each one. A set chosen for a pane in a menu or with the shortcut, including KTPH007NoneKTPH008, still wins for that pane. The same section has a master switch that turns highlighting off everywhere and greys out the menus, and an option to highlight inside full-screen programs such as KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002, which stays off by default because they redraw constantly. The default rule set is KTPH009NoneKTPH010, so nothing changes until you choose one, and every change applies to open terminals as soon as you save. See KTPH011Default rule set and settingsKTPH012.

KTPH000Your own highlighting rule setsKTPH001 — the new rule-set editor (KTPH002View → Highlighting → Manage Rule Sets…KTPH003, the KTPH004HighlightingKTPH005 submenu of the terminal context menu, or KTPH006Edit Rules…KTPH007 in KTPH008Settings → TerminalKTPH009) creates and changes rule sets of your own: words or regular expressions, whole word and ignore case, the matched text or the whole line, a theme or custom text and background color, and bold, italic or underline, in a priority order you set. The built-in sets stay read-only, and KTPH010DuplicateKTPH011 turns one into an editable copy. A live preview shows a test text the way a terminal pane would, with the hits of each rule and a warning for a rule that is slow or runs out of its time limit, and KTPH012OKKTPH013 stays disabled while a rule cannot work. Your sets appear in the highlighting menus and as the default rule set as soon as you confirm the editor. See KTPH014Your own rule setsKTPH015.

KTPH001A highlighting rule set per connectionKTPH002 — the connection editor's KTPH003Terminal SettingsKTPH004 tab has a new KTPH005Terminal behaviorKTPH006 section where KTPH007Keyword highlightingKTPH008 picks the rule set that connection's terminals show, for example KTPH009Network devicesKTPH010 for your switches: KTPH011Use the defaultKTPH012 follows KTPH013Settings → TerminalKTPH014, KTPH015NoneKTPH016 keeps the connection plain even when a default is set, or pick a built-in set or one of your own. A pane shows the set chosen for it in a menu or with the shortcut first, then its connection's set, then the default. Saving in the Connection Manager applies the change to open terminals in every window, a split to another server follows that server's connection, and the choice is stored in KTPH000 and survives duplicating, exporting and importing; a set that does not exist on this computer, for example from a shared teamwork file, is skipped. See KTPH017Rule set per connectionKTPH018.

KTPH002Rename terminal tabsKTPH003 — right-click a tab and choose KTPH004Rename Tab…KTPH005, or use KTPH006File → Rename Tab…KTPH007, to give a terminal tab a name of its own in place of the connection's name; the coding-agent glyph, the tab group and the KTPH000 marker stay. An empty name shows the connection's name again. Projects save the name and restore it, and the Coding Agents panel and the Control API's KTPH001 show it. See KTPH008Working with tabsKTPH009.

KTPH000Close other tabs or the tabs to the rightKTPH001 — right-click a terminal tab and choose KTPH002Close Other TabsKTPH003 or KTPH004Close Tabs to the RightKTPH005, or use the KTPH006FileKTPH007 menu entries of the same name for the active tab. The tab you chose stays open and becomes the active tab. Rather than one question per tab you are asked at most once, and only when some of the closing terminals have split panes or a command that is still running; an editor with unsaved changes still asks on its own, and a Cancel keeps every tab open. See KTPH008Working with tabsKTPH009.

KTPH021Jump to a tab with Cmd/Ctrl+1 to 9KTPH022 — KTPH023KTPH000KTPH024+KTPH025KTPH001KTPH026 to KTPH027KTPH002KTPH028+KTPH029KTPH003KTPH030 on macOS and KTPH031KTPH004KTPH032+KTPH033KTPH005KTPH034 to KTPH035KTPH006KTPH036+KTPH037KTPH007KTPH038 on Windows and Linux select the first to eighth tab of the window, and KTPH039KTPH008KTPH040+KTPH041KTPH009KTPH042 / KTPH043KTPH010KTPH044+KTPH045KTPH011KTPH046 the last one, with the top-row or the numpad digits and also while a terminal has the focus. No digit is left behind in the terminal or mirrored to the other panes in broadcast mode. On Windows and Linux only KTPH047KTPH012KTPH048 with a digit jumps, so KTPH049KTPH013KTPH050 characters and KTPH051KTPH014KTPH052+KTPH053KTPH015KTPH054+KTPH055KTPH016KTPH056 still reach the terminal, while KTPH057KTPH017KTPH058+KTPH059KTPH018KTPH060 to KTPH061KTPH019KTPH062+KTPH063KTPH020KTPH064 themselves no longer do (the terminal never sent them as keys of their own). See KTPH065Keyboard shortcutsKTPH066.

KTPH008Reopen closed tabsKTPH009 — KTPH010KTPH000KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH002KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH003KTPH017 on macOS and KTPH018KTPH004KTPH019+KTPH020KTPH005KTPH021+KTPH022KTPH006KTPH023+KTPH024KTPH007KTPH025 on Windows and Linux, KTPH026File → Reopen Closed TabKTPH027 or KTPH028Reopen Closed TabKTPH029 in a terminal tab's right-click menu bring back the terminal tab you closed last, with a new session to the same connection and with its tab group, its name and its terminal effect; its output and split panes are not restored. KTPH030File → Recently ClosedKTPH031 lists the last 25 closes, newest first: a single tab, the tabs one KTPH032Close Other TabsKTPH033, KTPH034Close Tabs to the RightKTPH035 or KTPH036Close All TabsKTPH037 closed, which reopen together, or the tabs of a window you closed while korTTY kept running. Tabs whose session ended on their own and everything that closes when you quit are not listed. A reopened tab signs in like KTPH038ConnectKTPH039 in the Connection Manager, with the saved connection as it is now and the server access policy checked first; the list never keeps a temporary SSH key, so a session that used one asks for a new key. The KTPH040Close all tabs?KTPH041 question no longer says this cannot be undone. See KTPH042Working with tabsKTPH043.

KTPH002Open recent connections and projectsKTPH003 — KTPH004File → Open RecentKTPH005 lists the saved connections you used last and the projects you opened or saved last, so you get back to them without the Connection Manager or the file dialog. Under KTPH006ConnectionsKTPH007 are up to 10 connections, newest first, as at the top of Quick Connect; choosing one opens a tab that signs in like KTPH008ConnectKTPH009 in the Connection Manager, with the server access policy checked first. Under KTPH010ProjectsKTPH011 are up to 10 project files, followed by the other projects in KTPH000; choosing one opens it like KTPH012File → Open Project…KTPH013, and a file that was moved or deleted is left out. KTPH014Clear ListKTPH015 empties the menu without deleting a connection or a project file. The paths of the recent projects are kept in KTPH001, so they are part of configuration backups. See KTPH016Open RecentKTPH017.

KTPH000Split panes come back with a project, on their own serversKTPH001 — opening a project rebuilt a tab's split panes only after a fixed one-second wait during which the window froze, then showed a KTPH002ConnectingKTPH003 dialog for every pane, put every pane on the tab's server even when it had been opened on another one, and could put the panes of a nested layout in the wrong places with the dividers in the middle. The panes now open once the tab is connected, one after the other in the background, each in its saved place with the saved divider positions. A pane opened on another server comes back on that server, signing in with what is stored, and every pane passes the server access policy. A pane that would need a password, a new temporary key, a locked vault or a blocked server stays closed with the panes split from it, and the status bar says how many panes were not reopened and why. korTTY drops a pane's working directory and scrollback reference from every project file it opens or saves, so a shared project cannot choose the folder a local shell starts in. See KTPH004Split panesKTPH005.

KTPH000Projects keep every window and its active tabKTPH001 — KTPH002File → Save ProjectKTPH003 saved only the window you chose it in, and KTPH004File → Open ProjectKTPH005 put the tabs of every saved window into one window, ignored which tab had been active and set the saved bounds without checking that the screen was still there. A project now keeps every open window with its position, size and maximized state, its tabs and the tab that was active. Opening it gives the first window to the window you open it from and opens each further window in a new window, while the windows already open keep their tabs; a project file holding several windows therefore no longer lands in one window. A window whose screen is no longer attached opens centred on the main screen, the tabs come back in their saved order and tab groups, and each window selects its active tab, also when that is a remote file that is still downloading. See KTPH006WindowsKTPH007.

KTPH000Projects reopen local shells and list the tabs that need you in one barKTPH001 — opening a project skipped every local shell tab, because its authentication field says "password" by default, and silently skipped every tab whose password was not saved or sat in the locked vault; an expired temporary SSH key was renewed without asking. Opening a project now asks nothing while it opens the tabs: local shells, SSH key logins, saved passwords and valid temporary keys open right away, and every other tab is listed in a bar above the status line of its window, for example KTPH002Tabs not reopened: sign-in needed (2) · vault locked (1)KTPH003, which never blocks the window. KTPH004Connect…KTPH005 asks for each missing password or new temporary key once per connection and opens the tabs with their saved screen, group, name and split panes, KTPH006Unlock Vault…KTPH007 opens the tabs whose password is in the vault (in every window, also when you unlock the vault from the menu), KTPH008DetailsKTPH009 names every tab and why it did not open, and KTPH010DismissKTPH011 forgets them. Servers the server access policy blocks, deleted connections and missing local files are listed there instead of being skipped or shown one dialog at a time. A temporary SSH key that korTTY could not decrypt because the vault was locked at startup now counts as one that needs renewing, here and wherever you connect, instead of starting an SSH key login without a key. See KTPH012Tabs that wait for youKTPH013.

KTPH001Restore the previous sessionKTPH002 — korTTY now saves your open windows and tabs while it runs, a couple of seconds after each change and once more when you quit, and KTPH003File → Restore Previous SessionKTPH004 opens what was open before this start, after a restart or a crash: every window with its position, size, tabs, split panes and active tab. The tabs open like those of a project with Auto-Reconnect and ask nothing; a tab that needs a password, a new temporary SSH key or the locked vault waits in the restore bar. No screen text, scrollback, password or temporary SSH key is saved, the files in KTPH000 are readable only by you and are not part of backups, and a session without tabs never replaces the previous one. The Recently Closed list now survives a restart as well, kept as the ids of saved connections only. See KTPH005Previous sessionKTPH006.

KTPH000The previous session is offered at startupKTPH001 — when korTTY starts, a bar above the status line now offers the windows and tabs that were open before, for example KTPH002Restore the windows and tabs from before this start? Windows: 2, tabs: 6KTPH003, with KTPH004RestoreKTPH005 and KTPH006DismissKTPH007; it never blocks the window, and nothing opens until you choose. KTPH008Settings → Window → Session RestoreKTPH009 can restore them automatically instead, as soon as no dialog such as the question about anonymous data is open, or do nothing at startup; KTPH010File → Restore Previous SessionKTPH011 works in every mode. If you neither restore nor dismiss the offer and open nothing yourself, the next start offers it again, and a second korTTY started while the first one runs never offers it. If korTTY ends unexpectedly within a minute of a restore, the next start asks instead of restoring automatically, so a session that makes korTTY crash cannot do so at every start. See KTPH012At startupKTPH013.

KTPH002Local shells restart in their last folderKTPH003 — after a restart, KTPH004File → Restore Previous SessionKTPH005 and the startup restore opened every local shell in its home folder or the connection's working directory, so you had to KTPH000 back into your project in each tab and pane. The session snapshot now keeps the folder each local shell was in, and the restored shell starts there, as long as the folder still exists; nothing is typed into the shell. SSH and Mosh tabs never get a KTPH001, and project files still never carry a folder. See KTPH006Local shells start where you left themKTPH007.

KTPH000Restore the output of your terminals, encryptedKTPH001 — a restored session opened every terminal empty, so the output you had been reading before a restart or a crash was gone. The new option KTPH002Settings → Window → Session Restore → Also restore the output of each terminal paneKTPH003 keeps the newest lines of every pane (1,000 by default, 100 to 5,000) and shows them again, dimmed and between two marker rows, above the new session of the restored tab or pane; it is only shown locally and never sent to the server or typed into the shell. See KTPH006Restoring the outputKTPH007.

KTPH008Command paletteKTPH009 — KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 on macOS, KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019+KTPH020KTPH006KTPH021 on Windows and Linux, or KTPH022View → Command Palette…KTPH023 opens a search box over every command of the window's menus: type a few letters of a name, or of its menu path (KTPH000 finds KTPH024View › Live Journal › Dock LeftKTPH025), and press KTPH026KTPH007KTPH027 to run it exactly as its menu item would. It has no shortcut by default, since KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH002KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH003KTPH013 belongs to the JobScheduler; give it one in KTPH014Settings → KeyboardKTPH015 and that shortcut also works while a terminal has the focus. KTPH009Ctrl+Tab in the order you last used the tabsKTPH010 — KTPH011KTPH000KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH001KTPH014 can now go back to the tab you used before the current one instead of the next tab of the tab bar, so one press switches between your two latest tabs wherever they sit. Turn on KTPH015Settings → Window → Tabs → Ctrl+Tab switches tabs in the order they were last usedKTPH016; then keep KTPH017KTPH002KTPH018 held and press KTPH019KTPH003KTPH020 again to go further back, add KTPH021KTPH004KTPH022 to step the other way, and release KTPH023KTPH005KTPH024 at the tab you want, which is the only one that counts as used. See KTPH031Window settingsKTPH032.

KTPH002Tab titles from the shellKTPH003 — a terminal tab now shows the title its shell or program sets with OSC 0 or OSC 2, such as KTPH000 from the default KTPH001 of Debian and Ubuntu, in place of the connection's name; a tab with split panes follows the pane that has the focus, and a name you gave the tab with KTPH004Rename TabKTPH005 still comes first. Pointing at such a tab shows the connection it belongs to. The server decides this title, so korTTY strips control and bidi characters from it, caps it at 80 characters and never lets it change the tab color or the frame; it is not saved in projects. To keep the connection's names, switch off KTPH006Name terminal tabs after the title the shell setsKTPH007 in KTPH008Settings → WindowKTPH009. See KTPH010Title from the shellKTPH011.

KTPH002Links in terminal output keep their colorsKTPH003 — text inside a clickable OSC 8 link was drawn in the terminal's default text color whenever the mouse was not over it, and terminal recordings stored it without its colors and bold. Linked text now keeps the colors it was printed with and is underlined while you hold KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 (macOS) or KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007 (Windows, Linux) over it, and recordings also keep its bold and inverse video. See KTPH008Links in terminal outputKTPH009.

KTPH000Links keep bold, italic, inverse video and color changesKTPH001 — on screen, text inside an OSC 8 link lost its bold, italic and inverse video, a color change in the middle of a link was ignored, resetting the text attributes inside a link ended the link, and a selection or search match on a link was not highlighted. With the terminal engine SithTermFX 1.2.3, linked text shows exactly the colors and attributes the program printed, on screen and in recordings, and a selection or search match on it is highlighted like other text. A window title or other OSC string longer than 64 Ki characters is now ignored instead of being applied cut off. See KTPH002Links in terminal outputKTPH003.

KTPH004Terminal links open only with Cmd/Ctrl+clickKTPH005 — a plain click on a link that a program printed opened it at once, a double-click opened it twice, and a selection dragged across the screen opened the link it ended on, even while tmux or vim was using the mouse. Links now open only on a single KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007 + click (macOS) or KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 + click (Windows, Linux) that does not move the mouse; a plain click on a link does nothing, a double-click selects its word and a triple-click its line as on other text, and KTPH010KTPH002KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH003KTPH013 (AltGr on Windows) with a click never opens a link. See KTPH014Links in terminal outputKTPH015.

KTPH003Cmd/Ctrl+click opens web and e-mail addresses printed as plain textKTPH004 — only links that a program marked up with OSC 8 could be opened, so the addresses in log lines, compiler messages and KTPH000 hints had to be copied into the browser by hand. A KTPH005KTPH001KTPH006 + click (macOS) or KTPH007KTPH002KTPH008 + click (Windows, Linux) now also opens a web address printed as plain text in the browser and an e-mail address as a new mail, with the same allowlist as OSC 8 links and also when the address wraps over several rows; a plain click still selects text as before. korTTY looks for the address only when you click, so terminal output is not slowed down, and it never opens an address cut short. Detection is on by default and can be switched off under KTPH009Settings → Terminal → LinksKTPH010. See KTPH011Links in terminal outputKTPH012.

KTPH001Terminal links show where they go before you open themKTPH002 — the text of a link that a program printed could hide its real target, and nothing showed that a web address in plain text could be opened at all. Resting the mouse on a link now shows the hand cursor, an underline and, after half a second, a tooltip with KTPH003Cmd+click to openKTPH004 or KTPH005Ctrl+click to openKTPH006 and the address the link really opens, with international host names in their KTPH000 form and hidden control and bidi characters made visible. When the text of a link shows a web address on another host than the link opens, a Cmd/Ctrl+click asks first, with KTPH007CancelKTPH008 as the default answer. See KTPH009Links in terminal outputKTPH010.

KTPH002Open Link and Copy Link Address in the terminal's right-click menuKTPH003 — opening a terminal link needed KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 or KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007 held down, and copying the address behind an OSC 8 link was not possible at all, because only its text could be selected. Right-clicking a link now puts KTPH008Open LinkKTPH009 and KTPH010Copy Link AddressKTPH011 at the top of the context menu: KTPH012Open LinkKTPH013 opens it like a Cmd/Ctrl+click, the question for a link whose text shows another host included, and KTPH014Copy Link AddressKTPH015 copies the address the link really opens, or a plain-text address as printed. A link korTTY does not open gets neither entry. See KTPH016Links in terminal outputKTPH017.

KTPH007Quick select copies or opens what the terminal shows with a few keysKTPH008 — copying an address, a path, a commit hash or a process ID out of terminal output needed the mouse. KTPH009KTPH000KTPH010+KTPH011KTPH001KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014 (macOS) or KTPH015KTPH003KTPH016+KTPH017KTPH004KTPH018+KTPH019KTPH005KTPH020 (Windows, Linux), or KTPH021Edit → Quick SelectKTPH022, now marks every web address, file path, e-mail address, UUID, IP address, git hash and number of four or more digits in the focused pane with a label of one or two letters, starting at the bottom row: typing a label copies its text, and KTPH023KTPH006KTPH024 with the label opens a web or e-mail address like a Cmd/Ctrl+click. Nothing typed while quick select runs reaches the program, in broadcast mode or through an input method neither, and copies respect the internal clipboard mode. See KTPH025Quick selectKTPH026.

KTPH003Quick select with your own patterns and label lettersKTPH004 — quick select only labelled what it knew, web addresses, paths, e-mail and IP addresses, hashes and long numbers, with fixed label letters, so a ticket number or a host name still had to be copied with the mouse. KTPH005Settings → Terminal → LinksKTPH006 now takes regular expressions of your own, one per line, whose matches quick select labels too, such as KTPH000 for KTPH001, and the letters its labels are made of. A pattern match at least as long as a built-in match it overlaps wins, so KTPH002 is offered whole instead of the number in it. A pattern that is not valid, matches empty text or is too long, and letters that are repeated, uppercase or no letters at all, are explained under their field and cannot be saved, and a pattern that takes too long on what the screen shows is skipped for that quick select instead of freezing the window. See KTPH007Your own patterns and label lettersKTPH008.

KTPH013File paths and KTPH000 links in terminal output open in the Snippet EditorKTPH014 — a path in a compiler message, a KTPH001 hit or a log line had to be copied and opened by hand, and the KTPH002 links that KTPH003, KTPH004 or KTPH005 put on file names did nothing. In SSH and local-shell tabs a KTPH015KTPH010KTPH016 + click (macOS) or KTPH017KTPH011KTPH018 + click (Windows, Linux) on such a path, KTPH019Open File in Snippet EditorKTPH020 in the right-click menu, or KTPH021KTPH012KTPH022 with its quick-select label now opens the file as text in the Snippet Editor, read over SFTP or from disk: absolute paths, KTPH006, and relative paths against the shell's current directory, without the KTPH007 after them. It never starts a program, only regular UTF-8 text files of up to 10 MB open, on the server as on your disk, network paths such as KTPH008 are never read, and a KTPH009 link opens read-only and only when it names the session's own host. Paths follow the KTPH023Open in Snippet EditorKTPH024 policy and the setting under KTPH025Settings → Terminal → LinksKTPH026. See KTPH027Links in terminal outputKTPH028.

KTPH000The menu bar of a closed macOS window acts in a window you can seeKTPH001 — korTTY keeps running on macOS after you close its last window, and the menu bar at the top of the screen still belonged to that closed window. KTPH002File → New TabKTPH003, KTPH004Connections → Manage Connections...KTPH005, KTPH006File → Open Project...KTPH007 and the other entries acted in the closed, hidden window, so nothing visible happened. They now act in the korTTY window you used last, which comes to the front, or open a new window first when none is open. Closing tabs or the window and KTPH008Edit → CutKTPH009, KTPH010CopyKTPH011 and KTPH012PasteKTPH013 do nothing from such a menu bar; KTPH014New WindowKTPH015 and KTPH016QuitKTPH017 work as before. See KTPH018macOS Dock KTPH020 menu barKTPH019.

KTPH000The terminal bell marks tabs you are not looking atKTPH001 — korTTY swallowed the terminal bell, so a build script or a prompt that rang it in a background tab went unnoticed. Such a tab now shows 🔔 in its title until you select it or bring its window to the front, and KTPH002Settings → Terminal → NotificationsKTPH003 can add a desktop notification titled with the tab's name, at most one per pane every 10 seconds (one for all panes of a multi-exec, and none for a bell that answers keys mirrored from another pane). The notification is off by default because shells ring on every failed Tab completion, it never contains terminal output, and a pane with a detected coding agent leaves the notice to the agent's own notification. See KTPH004Terminal notificationsKTPH005.

KTPH012Jump between prompts with shell integrationKTPH013 — finding where an earlier command and its output start in a long session meant scrolling and reading. With a few lines in the shell's startup file, which the guide has for bash, zsh and fish, the shell marks every prompt and command (OSC 133), and KTPH014KTPH000KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH001KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH002KTPH019 / KTPH020KTPH003KTPH021+KTPH022KTPH004KTPH023+KTPH024KTPH005KTPH025 (KTPH026KTPH006KTPH027+KTPH028KTPH007KTPH029+KTPH030KTPH008KTPH031 / KTPH032KTPH009KTPH033+KTPH034KTPH010KTPH035+KTPH036KTPH011KTPH037 on Windows and Linux), KTPH038Edit → Previous Prompt / Next PromptKTPH039 or the terminal's right-click menu jump from prompt to prompt in the focused pane. Without the marks, and while a full-screen program runs, the keys reach the program as before; a pane without marks offers KTPH040Set Up Shell Integration…KTPH041 in its right-click menu, and KTPH042Settings → Terminal → Shell integrationKTPH043 switches the feature off. See KTPH044Shell integrationKTPH045.

KTPH002Set Up Shell Integration…KTPH003, in the right-click menu of a terminal whose shell sends no marks and as a button in KTPH004Settings → Terminal → Shell integrationKTPH005, now opens a window with the snippets for bash, zsh and fish, where each one goes and a KTPH006CopyKTPH007 button; from a local shell tab it opens on that shell's snippet. The window stays open while you paste into a terminal, and KTPH008CopyKTPH009 goes through korTTY's clipboard, so the internal clipboard mode of the enterprise policy keeps the snippet inside korTTY. korTTY still never changes files on a server or types into an SSH session to set this up. See KTPH010Setting it upKTPH011.

KTPH011Shell integration for local shells without touching a startup fileKTPH012 — using shell integration in a local shell tab meant pasting korTTY's snippet into KTPH000, KTPH001 or fish's KTPH002 by hand. KTPH013Add shell integration automaticallyKTPH014, on the KTPH015ConnectionKTPH016 tab of a local shell connection, now starts bash, zsh or fish with a startup file of korTTY's own that runs yours first and then the snippet: through KTPH003 for bash, also for a login bash such as Git Bash, a KTPH004 folder that hands your own KTPH005 back for zsh, and KTPH006 for fish, also from the Flatpak package. Your startup files are never changed; the wrapper is readable only by you, lives in KTPH007 and is deleted when the tab closes. It is off until you tick it, works for shells started with no other options than KTPH008, KTPH009 and KTPH010, and is never used for SSH or Mosh connections or for connections shared through Teamwork, and an export leaves it behind; the Set Up Shell Integration window points to it. See KTPH017Adding it to local shells automaticallyKTPH018.

KTPH000Select or copy the last command's outputKTPH001 — getting the output of a command out of the terminal meant dragging over it with the mouse, line by line through the scrollback for a long one. In a shell set up for shell integration, KTPH002Edit → Select Last OutputKTPH003 and KTPH004Edit → Copy Last OutputKTPH005, also in the terminal's right-click menu, now take everything the last finished command printed, without its prompt and command line: Select marks it like a mouse selection, Copy puts it on the clipboard and leaves your selection alone, through the internal clipboard mode when the policy sets it. When the start of a long output has left the scrollback, they take the rest and the status bar says so. See KTPH006Selecting and copying a command's outputKTPH007.

KTPH000Exit status and runtime in the timestamp sidebarKTPH001 — the command timestamp sidebar showed only times and the time between two of them, and it took a command to be finished after half a second without new output, so a command that paused before printing more was marked finished too early. In a shell set up for shell integration, the line where a command finished now shows ✓ for exit status 0 or a red ✗ for any other, the command's real runtime next to the date and the time it finished as the shell reported it; pointing at the line shows the exit status and the runtime, and a command that still runs shows … on the first line of its output. The sidebar is off by default: turn it on with KTPH002View → Show Command TimestampsKTPH003. See KTPH004Exit status and runtimeKTPH005.

KTPH000A notification when a long command finishesKTPH001 — a build or an upgrade left running in a background tab gave no sign that it was done, so you kept switching back to check. In a shell set up for shell integration, a command that ran at least 30 seconds and finishes in a tab you are not looking at now marks that tab with 🔔 and shows a desktop notification titled with the tab's name that says whether the command finished or failed, with its exit status and runtime, never the command itself. KTPH002Settings → Terminal → NotificationsKTPH003 switches the notification off or sets the minimum runtime from 1 to 3,600 seconds; a tab notifies at most once every 10 seconds, so the same command finishing in several broadcast panes notifies once, a command typed once into the panes of a multi-exec notifies once for all of them, and commands of korTTY's AI Agent never notify. See KTPH004Long-running commandsKTPH005.

KTPH003Notifications from programs on the server (OSC 9 and OSC 777)KTPH004 — a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex running over SSH, or a script of your own, could ask the terminal for a desktop notification, but korTTY ignored the request, so an agent waiting for your answer in a background tab went unnoticed. A program that sends KTPH000 or KTPH001 in a tab you are not looking at now marks that tab with 🔔 and shows a desktop notification titled with korTTY and the tab's name, with the program's text below it. The text is cleaned of control and bidi characters and cut to length, a pane notifies at most once every 5 seconds and drops what comes in between, ConEmu's KTPH002 progress reports are ignored, and a pane with a detected coding agent leaves the notice to the agent's own notification. It is on by default and can be switched off in KTPH005Settings → Terminal → NotificationsKTPH006. See KTPH007Notifications from programsKTPH008.

KTPH000Programs on the server can copy to your clipboard (OSC 52), if you allow itKTPH001 — copying in vim, Neovim or tmux on a server only reached the server's own registers, because korTTY ignored the OSC 52 sequence these programs use to put text on the terminal's clipboard. With KTPH002Let programs in the terminal copy text to the clipboard (OSC 52)KTPH003 switched on in KTPH004Settings → TerminalKTPH005, such a copy now lands on your clipboard, up to 256 KiB at a time, and the status bar names the tab it came from. Programs can only write, never read the clipboard, since korTTY never answers the OSC 52 query; the internal clipboard mode of the enterprise policy keeps their copies inside korTTY, and korTTY's log records only their size. The setting is off by default, because any program whose output reaches the terminal could otherwise replace what you copied; while it is off, the status bar says when a program tried. See KTPH006Programs copying to the clipboardKTPH007.

KTPH000Watch a tab for activity or silenceKTPH001 — korTTY could not tell you that a quiet log in a background tab printed something new, or that a build without shell integration had stopped printing. Right-click a terminal tab and choose KTPH002Monitor for ActivityKTPH003 to get the tab's 🔔 mark and a desktop notification when output appears after at least 10 seconds of quiet while you are not looking at it, once until you look at the tab, or KTPH004Monitor for SilenceKTPH005 to get them when a pane that was printing stays without output for 30 seconds, adjustable from 5 to 3,600 seconds in KTPH006Settings → Terminal → NotificationsKTPH007. Both are off until you switch them on, also from the command palette, and are never saved; the notifications never contain terminal output, and the echo of keys that broadcast mode or multi-exec typed into a pane counts as no activity, so typing into many watched panes at once does not notify from each of them. See KTPH008Watching a tab for activity or silenceKTPH009.

KTPH003Highlight rules that notify youKTPH004 — a keyword highlighting rule of your own can now show a desktop notification and mark its tab with 🔔 when its pattern appears in new output in a tab you are not looking at, for example KTPH000 during a long backup: set its KTPH005ActionKTPH006 to KTPH007Desktop notificationKTPH008 in the rule-set editor and give it a KTPH009Rule nameKTPH010. The notification is titled KTPH001 and the tab's name and says only the rule's name, unless you tick KTPH011Include the matched textKTPH012, which adds the match cleaned of control characters and cut to 100 characters; each rule notifies at most once every 30 seconds per pane. Output that was already in the pane, such as a project's restored screen, the scrollback when you switch rule sets and full-screen programs, never notifies, and a notifying rule never types anything into the terminal. KTPH013Run actions of highlight rules (notifications, snippets)KTPH014 in KTPH015Settings → TerminalKTPH016 switches them all off, and administrators can forbid them with the new policy key KTPH002. See KTPH017Notifications for matching outputKTPH018.

KTPH002Highlight rules that run a snippetKTPH003 — a follow-up such as collecting diagnostics after KTPH000 had to be typed by hand, even when it was always the same snippet. A keyword highlighting rule can now run a snippet of the Snippet Manager in the pane where its pattern appears in new output: set its KTPH004ActionKTPH005 to KTPH006Run a snippetKTPH007 in the rule-set editor and pick the KTPH008SnippetKTPH009. korTTY asks before the first run in each connection, showing the rule, the snippet and its start, and the answer holds until you quit korTTY. A rule runs its snippet at most once every 30 seconds per pane, and after three runs in a row korTTY stops running snippets in that pane until 2 minutes pass without a match, so a snippet whose output matches its own rule cannot loop. The line you are typing at the prompt, output that answers broadcast or multi-exec keys, panes in which an agent works, restored screens and korTTY's own messages never run a snippet, the snippet goes to the matching pane only, and a rule never types text from the output or answers a prompt. The same setting and the policy key KTPH001 switch it off. See KTPH010Running a snippet when output matchesKTPH011.

KTPH001An invisible character can no longer reset all your settingsKTPH002 — a highlight rule's pattern or name, a rule set's name or an entry of the terminal agent's prompt history could hold a character that KTPH000 cannot store, such as a control character from a bracketed paste or U+FFFF; korTTY wrote it anyway, could not read the file at the next start and fell back to the default of every setting. KTPH000Connection groups, duplicated tabs and reconnects follow the server access policyKTPH001 — KTPH002Open GroupKTPH003 in Quick Connect opened every connection of the group without checking your organization's server allow or deny list, and KTPH004DuplicateKTPH005 on a tab did not check it either. See KTPH006Server access controlKTPH007.

KTPH001Review and replace a changed host keyKTPH002 — when a server was rebuilt, the changed-key alert of a terminal tab or the SFTP manager now offers KTPH003Review and Replace…KTPH004: it shows the trusted and the new SHA-256 fingerprint side by side and replaces the key only after you tick that you verified the new fingerprint with the server administrator. KTPH005CloseKTPH006 and KTPH007CancelKTPH008 stay the default buttons, background connections never offer the replacement, and the KTPH000 policy forbids it. The new KTPH009Configuration → Security → Known Hosts…KTPH010 lists, searches and removes trusted keys. See KTPH011SSH host-key verificationKTPH012.

KTPH004Import trusted host keys from OpenSSHKTPH005 — KTPH006Import from known_hosts...KTPH007 in KTPH008Configuration → Security → Known Hosts…KTPH009 reads KTPH000 or another file you pick and trusts the Ed25519, ECDSA and RSA keys of its hosts, including KTPH001 entries and host lists, after a confirmation. See KTPH010Importing OpenSSH known_hostsKTPH011.

KTPH000Split panes follow the server access policyKTPH001 — KTPH002Split Right (new connection)KTPH003 and KTPH004Split Down (new connection)KTPH005 connected to the server you picked without checking your organization's server allow or deny list, so a split pane could reach a server or jump server that Quick Connect and saved connections refuse. A blocked server or jump server is now refused right after you pick it, with the same policy message as Quick Connect and before korTTY asks for a password or saves the connection. Same-server splits check the policy too, so a tab whose saved connection was edited to point at a blocked server or jump server cannot open a pane there. See KTPH006Server access controlKTPH007.

KTPH000Open Group opens key-based connections and local shellsKTPH001 — KTPH002Open GroupKTPH003 in Quick Connect silently left out every connection of the group that had no saved password, so connections that log in with an SSH key and local shells never opened. A connection that logs in with a password and has none saved is still left out, but a message now names it, so you can open it on its own and enter the password.

KTPH000Connect checks the server policy before it asks for anything, and Duplicate signs in like the Connection ManagerKTPH001 — KTPH002ConnectKTPH003 in the Connection Manager asked for a password before it checked your organization's server allow or deny list, so you could type a password for a server korTTY then refused; the policy message now comes first. A password saved in the locked vault now offers KTPH004Unlock Vault…KTPH005, where Connect used to do nothing for a password saved with the connection and asked you to type one saved in a credential; if you do not unlock, korTTY asks for the password. The password dialog now belongs to the korTTY window and keeps KTPH006OKKTPH007 greyed out until you type something. A tab's KTPH008DuplicateKTPH009 now signs in the same way, so it reuses the tab's temporary SSH key while it is valid and asks for a new one once it has expired, where it used to ignore the key's expiry. See KTPH010Signing inKTPH011.

KTPH001A tab color per connectionKTPH002 — mark the tabs of a connection with a color, for example red for production servers: tick KTPH003Mark this connection's tabs with a colorKTPH004 in the new KTPH005Terminal behaviorKTPH006 section of the connection editor's KTPH007Terminal SettingsKTPH008 tab and pick a color. Every terminal tab of that connection then shows a colored dot in front of its title, and pointing at the tab names the connection and the color, which screen readers read as well. Saving in the Connection Manager updates the open tabs in every window; the yellow and dark red connection-status colors of a tab are unchanged. The color is stored in KTPH000, survives duplicating, exporting and importing, and can come with a shared teamwork connection. See KTPH009Tab colorKTPH010.

KTPH000A frame in the tab color around the terminalKTPH001 — the terminal of a connection with a tab color now also gets a 3-pixel frame of that color, around all of its split panes and status bars, so a production server stands out right where you type. Connections without a tab color are unchanged. If you prefer only the dot on the tab, switch off KTPH002Frame the terminal in its connection's tab colorKTPH003 in the new KTPH004TabsKTPH005 section of KTPH006Settings → WindowKTPH007; the change reaches the open tabs of every window at once. KTPH001Tab colors for credential environmentsKTPH002 — give a credential environment a tab color under KTPH003Configuration → Security → Credentials… → Environments...KTPH004: select the environment, tick KTPH005Mark this environment's tabs with a colorKTPH006 and pick a color. Right-click a folder in the Connection Manager and choose KTPH003Tab Color...KTPH004 to give every connection in it, and in its subfolders, a tab color; a subfolder or a connection with a color of its own keeps that one, and a folder color comes before the color of a credential environment. Renaming a folder keeps its color, deleting it removes the color, and no folder has a color until you pick one. Folder colors are saved in KTPH000 and never apply to teamwork connections. See KTPH005Tab colorKTPH006.

KTPH000A frame for split panes of another connectionKTPH001 — a pane that KTPH002Split Right (new connection)KTPH003 or KTPH004Split Down (new connection)KTPH005 opened to a connection with a different tab color sat inside its tab's frame and showed the tab's color, so a production pane in a test server's tab looked like the rest of the tab. A connection without a choice follows KTPH019Settings → Terminal → Paste protectionKTPH020, the size check always does, and the paste confirmation says when the connection set the warning. Each pane follows its own connection, so a split to another server uses that server's choice, and saving in the Connection Manager applies to the next paste into open terminals. Both values are stored in KTPH000 and survive duplicating, exporting and importing; a connection from a shared teamwork file can only make the warning ask more often, never switch it off. See KTPH021Paste protectionKTPH022.

KTPH005SSH tunnels now really openKTPH006 — tunnels configured on a connection were saved, imported and shared, but never opened. korTTY now opens the enabled ones once per terminal tab after login, closes them before a reconnect and opens them again afterwards, moves them to another pane of the same server when you close the pane they run on, and shows KTPH000 with the first error in the tab's status bar (hover for every tunnel). Because tunnels that never did anything would otherwise start listening silently after the update, korTTY asks once per connection before it opens them, and again when the tunnels or the server change. A remote tunnel listens on the SSH server's loopback address unless you name another one, shared (Teamwork) connections never open remote tunnels and may only listen on KTPH001, and administrators can forbid tunnels with the new KTPH002 policy key. Remote tunnels that earlier versions imported from PuTTY Connection Manager carry the bind address KTPH003; the confirmation, the tunnel list and the status bar mark them as reachable from other computers, so set their KTPH007Remote bind addressKTPH008 to KTPH004 if the forwarded port should stay private to the server. A value you picked in an earlier version, when it had no effect, is not applied on its own: SSH sessions stay UTF-8 until you save the settings after opening the Terminal page, where a note points this out. KTPH000Temporary SSH keys are no longer left in the temp folderKTPH001 — every connect, split and SFTP session with a temporary SSH key wrote the private key to a file in the system temp folder that was never deleted, so the key stayed on disk long after it had expired, and the debug log recorded the beginning and end of the key text. KTPH001Scheduled jobs keep temporary keys off the disk tooKTPH002 — a JobScheduler job with a temporary SSH key now authenticates in memory like a terminal tab. Only an Rsync job still needs the key as a file for its external KTPH000; that file is created owner-only from the start and deleted when the job ends or its connection fails, instead of staying in the temp folder.

KTPH005JMX monitoring shows the connections that are really openKTPH006 — the KTPH000 MBean always reported 0 active connections and no names, because it read a session list that nothing ever filled. KTPH001, KTPH002 and KTPH003 now list every live SSH and Mosh terminal connection (each split pane counts, local shells do not), and KTPH004, which was never measured, stays at 0 for existing JMX clients. See KTPH007Logging and diagnosticsKTPH008.

KTPH006Close TabKTPH007 (KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011, KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 on macOS), KTPH016Close All TabsKTPH017, opening a project and closing the window removed the tab but let a chat request run on to its answer and a swarm go on running its agents' commands on every server. Every way of closing the tab now cancels what it runs, as its KTPH018CancelKTPH019 or KTPH020StopKTPH021 button does. See KTPH022AI result tab featuresKTPH023 and KTPH024Run controlKTPH025.

The table shown when the AI cannot be reached stays unchanged because it never leaves your computer. The terminal, the activity panel, the approval dialog and the journal keep the real output, a KTPH004Masked before sendingKTPH005 entry in the activity panel counts the masked values, and a planned command that contains the KTPH001 placeholder is not run. See KTPH006Masking what the agent sendsKTPH007.

KTPH001One switch for the shell's prompt marksKTPH002 — KTPH003Settings → AIKTPH004 had KTPH005Use OSC 133 prompt markers when the shell already provides themKTPH006, which changed nothing: the AI Agent's KTPH000 commands and the question before closing a busy SSH tab read the marks either way. See KTPH011Shell integrationKTPH012.

See KTPH003AI SkillsKTPH004.

KTPH000All AI calls count towards the profile quotaKTPH001 — session journal calls, every AI Swarm agent and the swarm's combined answer, and scheduled AI jobs were not added to the profile's token quota before; they now are, so the quota bar reflects what was really spent.
